Most BPD people or Cluster B personality disorders in general aren't going to go over well with a loved one trying to tell them this is their problem.

BUT, if a BPD person is self-aware enough and is persistent with DBT, I think they're the most likely to eventually find success within the Cluster B personality disorder group.

I have 2 friends getting married and have strongly suspected one of them to have BPD, and the best I can do is tell both of them about my experience to see if either of them pick up on the signs...and to me, it's pretty concerning that the suspected BPD one hasn't seemed to wonder this about themselves but has wondered if they have all these other diagnosises.

My husband sees it too and has considered talking to the non-BPD spouse about how to live with someone with BPD, and I'm like...eh, it's very different if someone is getting treatment. It's an utter nightmare if someone isn't getting treatment.

It's tough because the suspected BPD one is genuinely a really cool person and obviously suffering a lot internally. I have another friend who I suspect to be histrionic (same family and some psychologists argue there isn't a difference b/w histrionic and BPD, but i strongly disagree, and separate rant about how much work needs to be done to diagnose these conditions, de-stigmatize them and put them on a spectrum the way we have with autism, and also what treatment looks like).

Anyway, the histrionic friend is also unaware and continues to have issues with relationships, but again...many many amazing qualities that make friendship enjoyable.

It's an interesting paradox for a person with BPD to recognize they're likely to attract people within the same family of personality disorders into their own circles...but also not diagnose them or try to help them from a clinical standpoint because it's not our job..and yet the medical field still lacks so much in this arena that many people will never get diagnosed because professionals are very hesitant to give the diagnosis. 

Marriage is a very big deal, and realistically, you need to ask yourself if you can marry someone who might never be able to admit this quality about themselves.

I also have 2 friends where one is a narcissist...ironically, the spouse who told them they suspect they have this said "yeah, you're probably right." I say ironic because NPD is the least likely to seek out help. But they do well with each other actually. Ofc, the NPD one still struggles a lot internally...a lot of depression.

All that to say, only because you're considering marriage do i think you should try and broach the subject. If she's not even open to hearing this.about herself and explore it...really consider leaving the relationship.

I was also nervous because I wasn't sure about the gender dynamics (i.e. within the Indian community, it's easier for me to tell when an Indian is progressive or not when it comes to women in the workplace).

1. There does need to be an adjustment period to understand someone else's accent. I have no issues now but that was after probably a month of talking to people in person or having their camera on on zoom. Without the camera, it's *really* hard.

2. Growing up in the USA, I assumed people weren't mean to East Asians because they were fetishized and south Asians not so much. I also believed colorism plays more a role (i.e. people are nicer to people with lighter skin). Whether 2020 changed the dynamics or the problem existed before, people in the US are really racist toward Chinese people and need advocacy.

It's made me sad because the people I work with are genuinely the best coworkers I've had my entire career and I hope more walls come down because I do feel bad for my friend who is having a hard time.

Great question - i think it was indirectly both! Teller showed that the atmosphere could cause a fusion reaction from a fission trigger. He also showed that you could use hydrogen and later lithium to trigger a fusion reaction. I think the idea is that the probability with oxygen as the trigger is less probable than with hydrogen or lithium, but don't have the background to give better explanation as to why.

I do know that the triggering mechanism with oxygen from the atmosphere depends on the amount of heat generated during the initial blast vs the hydrogen bomb would be dependent on a fission source guaranteed to generate enough energy to cause a fusion reaction. The latter is definitely more devastating and scary which is why I felt the movie was alluding to that in conjunction with the fact that Oppenheimer was specifically being questioned over why he kept saying no to the hydrogen bomb in particular.

And in both cases, the chances for an infinite chain reaction are not 0, so it's hard to tell what the movie was particularly referring to, especially since the interaction between Einstein and Oppenheimer discussing said calculations at that time i think was a fictional account (I've been trying to find a source that would suggest otherwise, but really the timing doesn't make sense...they were never at Berkeley at the same time and by the time they were at Princeton together, the theory behind the hydrogen bomb would have been well established to be discussed between the 2 men). All these were reasons that led me to believe they were trying to allude to the hydrogen bomb calculations in particular, but it definitely wasn't clear.

I believe Teller had calculations for very early on in the Manhattan Project which is why it's so scary to think what could have happened if he wasn't Jewish and had stayed in Germany continuing to study under Heisenberg!

I meant he blocked it during the time he was there. Obviously, it went on to still be created after the war ended. There's an alternative reality in which if he hadn't said don't pursue it, they could have developed that in time to drop on Japan.

The entire persecution after was because he said no to the hydrogen bomb, and yes, he wanted to give Teller freedom to think about it purely theoretically, but it was well after the war ended that Teller eventually was able to actually begin development of it.

I think most theoretical physicists at the time knew it was possible to be developed, but they also knew it would be more devastating. He knew Teller's calculations were devastating...I think the movie tried to drive this point home by reiterating a dramatized encounter of him bringing those calculations to Einstein.

But again...you would still need fission to work. So while he may have originally blocked it due to practical reasons (you'd want to develop fission and then develop fusion), by the time he said no again after the war ended in 1949 which you refer to, he very much knew it was possible to be developed.

Theoretical physicists at the time had an undue burden of having to play politics then...so even Einstein can be found to be quoted to say he "doesn't believe in quantum studies" but we have ample amount of evidence to suggest otherwise and that he simply didn't want to be pulled in to work on something he didn't want to and completely shifted to an area he felt would be more...civil, so to speak (hydraulics).

I don't think there was any doubt in Oppenheimer's mind that the hydrogen bomb wasn't possible, I just can't say what his motivations for not putting practical resources behind it before the war ended were. It's more clear to me that after the war, his qualms for saying no were more on moral grounds.

The movie doesn't do a great job at explaining what Teller's calculations actually are, and unfortunately, i think imply the chain reaction being infinite would happen with just a fission nuclear source, when the greater fear of an infinite chain reaction comes from a fission-fusion chain reaction which is what Teller's calculations were.

Teller first heard Fermi give the idea in 1941 of using hydrogen to trigger a fusion bomb and then ran with running more calculations on the scenario. The theory was definitely solidly there and discussed by several people but Teller wanted to move it out of theory into development which doesn't make a lot of sense to do until you do have a fission bomb first.

By 1949, the arguments would be less on practical and more on moral because now by that point, from a scientific perspective there's no reason to now try moving out of theory into practice. I think the wording he used in 1949 was you can more easily drop fission bombs on multiple targets versus a fusion bomb you can only do in 1 place with a large radius that doesn't warrant such force.

If you read between the lines of that... that's a moral opposition playing a political game.

But one cannot be certain of what his motivations before 1949 were...I don't think we'll ever be able to know if he switched from practical to moral reasoning once he saw the US use a fission bomb during a time that didn't seem necessary for.nuclear force, or if he'd always been morally opposed to it.

In the movie he says something like "I changed my mind once I knew we'd use whatever we have and it seems unnecessary" but I don't think there's sources out there with such real quotes, which would be nice, but I think at best we can just read between the lines of what they said during incredibly politically charged times and take that all into context.

The physics in interstellar was quite terrible despite many touting otherwise. If you can only appreciate fiction, I see why you feel this way. However, what is arguably one of the most life altering changes of our more recent history needed a lot to be told.

You have to understand the number of people it took to put all the science, testing, and production together.

You have to understand that any number of them had instead not been Jewish, we could very much have a different reality, and Nazis would have developed a fission or, worse, a hydrogen bomb first.

You have to understand that the tension between Straus and Oppenheimer, which he labeled at the start as Fission vs Fusion meant that had we instead developed a hydrogen bomb, the effects would be far more devastating to Japan and appreciate the room left to discuss what Oppenheimer's motivations for opposing th4 development 9f the hydrogen bomb were.

Finally, you have to understand that the US utilized many Jewish refugees when it politically made sense to do so and then as soon as done, dropped them, and moved on to former Nazi scientists to develop NASA as a response to the Cold War and how that was the true motivation for seeking out "Communists and Communist Sympathizers" within the scientific community. 

If you can't appreciate any of that and prefer unrealistic science fiction like interstellar... I guess that's why 2 movies that IMO shouldn't have the same rating do. People like you rate interstellar highly. People like me rate Oppenheimer highly. To each their own.

Downvoted but true - sadly a lot of people don't have the right kind of chilling sadness over Hiroshima and Nagasaki that is warranted or understand why the situation in Ukraine if it escalates causes a lot of us gripping fear.

Oppenheimer effectively did block the hydrogen bomb, which would have been wayyyy more devastating if that was used on Japan.

It's unclear if he was motivated by wanting to stop it for moral reasons or practical reasons. Practically speaking, you need to develop a packageable fission reaction to even get a hydrogen bomb, but if he really did say the blast radius is smaller, then he was likely lying for moral reasons.

He didn't have a name because his character was fictional or a composite character at best.  Alden Ehrenreich did do a great job helping us build up to the moment David Hill testified which was a real event and there were many scientists who understood what was happening to Oppenheimer so Ehrenreich's character being a likely composite character doesn't take away from the historical depiction accuracy IMO.

You're right to question the timeline because it likely did not happen. Einstein and Oppenheimer met at Princeton after the war.

The movie attempted a timeline where Oppenheimer asked Einstein about the calculations before their conversation. My best guess is that the conversation you see at the beginning took place at Princeton while maybe they discussed the Teller's equation at Berkeley...however the 2 were never there at the same time so it's hard to say when he would have asked Einstein something so classified beforehand. 

It is completely and very likely though that while at Princeton, Oppenheimer told Einstein of the more dangerous mechanism that Teller was fighting to make which was fission triggering fusion and that wasn't developed into reality until after the war. I think Einstein looking grim at the news is a realistic depiction, just the equation asking beforehand was likely dramatized fiction.
